content: Parallel use of chest X-rays (CXR) and the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen (W4SS) is recommended to exclude active tuberculosis (TB) disease before initiating TB preventive treatment (TPT) in individuals with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Evidence from eight studies conducted in various countries, including Benin, Botswana, Brazil, Guinea, India, Kenya, Malawi, Myanmar, Peru, South Africa, and Zimbabwe, involving 6,238 participants, was reviewed to inform the 2021 TB screening guidelines. CXR alone demonstrated similar sensitivity and equal or higher specificity compared to the W4SS across all subpopulations. When CXR was performed after a positive W4SS, its sensitivity was either lower or similar, while its specificity was higher or similar. When used in parallel with W4SS, CXR showed higher or similar sensitivity and similar specificity. Recommendation 12 addresses the use of C-reactive protein (CRP) for TB screening in adults and adolescents with HIV. Evidence from six studies conducted in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda, involving 3,971 participants, was reviewed. CRP accuracy was assessed using cut-off values of >5 mg/L and >10 mg/L as indicators of TB disease. The cut-off of >5 mg/L was recommended due to its higher sensitivity and its status as the lowest threshold for abnormality in many clinical settings. A meta-analysis of individual patient data showed that CRP with a cut-off of >5 mg/L had similar sensitivity and higher or similar specificity compared to W4SS across all subpopulations. When CRP was combined with W4SS and used in parallel, it demonstrated similar or greater sensitivity and specificity than W4SS alone, depending on the cut-off threshold and subpopulation assessed. CRP was most accurate for outpatients not on ART, with a sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 37% in this group. When used sequentially after a positive W4SS in people with HIV not on ART, CRP with a cut-off of >5 mg/L maintained similar sensitivity (84%) but significantly improved specificity (64%). Recommendation 13 pertains to the use of molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) for TB screening in adults and adolescents with HIV. A systematic review of 14 studies involving 9,209 participants evaluated the performance of mWRDs, with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay being the most commonly used. The sensitivity of mWRDs alone was 69%, with a specificity of 98%. When W4SS was followed by mWRD testing, sensitivity was slightly lower at 62%, but specificity remained high at 99%. The accuracy of mWRDs was comparable to that of W4SS followed by mWRD testing across various subpopulations. For children under 15 years who are close contacts of individuals with TB, symptom-based screening (including cough, fever, or poor weight gain) was found to have a pooled sensitivity of 89% and specificity of 69%. CXR screening for abnormalities suggestive of TB in this group showed a pooled sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 91%. Among HIV-negative household contacts aged ≥5 years, the absence of TB symptoms and normal CXR findings can be used to rule out TB disease before initiating TPT. For individuals aged ≥15 years, systematic TB screening may involve symptom screening, CXR, or mWRDs, alone or in combination. The use of CXR in TB screening has been routine for decades, but its application is often limited by the availability of trained personnel and variability in interpretation. Computer-aided detection (CAD) systems can address these limitations and are conditionally recommended for TB screening and triage in individuals aged ≥15 years. The addition of CXR to symptom screening improves sensitivity but increases logistical and resource demands. Local authorities should determine the frequency and application of CXR based on local epidemiology and resources. For TB infection (TBI) testing, either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used. Both tests are considered equivalent, with no strong evidence favoring one over the other for predicting progression to TB disease. However, TST may require fewer resources and is more familiar in resource-limited settings, though global shortages and stock-outs can limit its scalability. IGRA testing is more costly and requires laboratory infrastructure, but it is less affected by prior Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination. New TB antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) have shown diagnostic accuracy similar to IGRAs and greater than TSTs, and they are recommended for all subpopulations, including people with HIV and children. In conclusion, TB screening and testing strategies should be tailored to local contexts, considering resource availability, infrastructure, and population needs. Symptom screening remains a critical and accessible tool, while the addition of CXR, CRP, or mWRDs can enhance diagnostic accuracy in specific settings.
